title: Supervisory Engineering Work
author: Annie Vella
description: Examines how AI coding assistants shift software engineers from manual code creation toward a new 'middle loop' of supervisory engineering—directing AI, verifying its output, and correcting it when wrong—connecting modern agentic workflows to classic human-factors supervisory control theory.

title: Take My Toil, Leave Me My Struggle
author: Kent Beck
description: Imagine RoboGym, where pressing a 'Lift' button moves weights up and down for you—missing the entire point of a workout. Kent Beck reflects on how AI 'Genies' are being designed as a RoboGym for the mind, arguing that tools should eliminate mechanical toil while preserving the cognitive struggle that builds human understanding and mastery.

title: Codecamp Cluj-Napoca 2026
author: Codecamp
description: 20 October 2026. Conference and masterclasses covering modern software architecture, AI engineering, and craftsmanship.

title: Someone behind the software
author: Karri Saarinen
description: Karri Saarinen reflects on craftsmanship in software, arguing that the best products carry the taste, care, and distinct point of view of the people who build them.

title: How the Claude Code team does code review
author: Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt & Qing Wang
description: How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents.

title: Trace agents with OpenTelemetry on the Claude Platform
author: Anthropic
description: Announcing OpenTelemetry traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs on the Claude Platform.

title: On the Death of Amazon’s Writing Culture
author: Steve Huynh
description: Former Amazon Principal Engineer Steve Huynh examines how generative AI broke the core guarantee behind Amazon's six-page narrative memo culture—that clear writing requires clear thinking—turning a rigorous engineering ritual into hollow, AI-generated prose.

title: Thinking will become a hobby
author: Diomidis Spinellis
description: Diomidis Spinellis reflects on the trajectory of AI systems outperforming human cognition across perception, reasoning, and autonomous action, arguing that driven by superior performance, lower cost, and 24/7 availability, professional thinking will increasingly be delegated to AI while human thinking becomes a hobby.

title: Why Agent-Written Code Needs Product Verification
author: Paul Stack
description: Whether your tests catch real defects is not a property of the test level. It is a property of where the expectations come from and who can change them. The expectations have to come from outside the implementation loop — and those expectations need to be protected.

title: What TLA+ can and can't check
author: Hillel Wayne
description: Let's chill just a little bit on the "TLA+ will save AI from itself" narrative. Hillel Wayne breaks down what TLA+ can express (invariants, action properties, liveness) and what it fundamentally cannot check natively—unformalizable domain concepts, multi-step safety without auxiliary variables, reachability, and hyperproperties across sets of behaviors.

title: GLM-5.3 and the spread of advanced cyber capabilities
author: Anthropic
description: GLM-5.3 can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits, but unlike other frontier models, it was released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse.

title: Uncle Bob: Why I Stopped Reading Code and Building Harnesses
author: Robert C. Martin
description: Uncle Bob, co-author of the Agile Manifesto and author of Clean Code, talks about why he stopped reading AI-generated code, the constraints that keep agents in line, and why only humans can be responsible for what agents produce.

title: Modern Solution Architecture with Barry O'Reilly
author: Barry O'Reilly
description: Monday, 14 September 2026, from 18.30 until 20.00 hrs (CEST). An interactive talk and masterclass session on modern solution architecture.

title: Java at 30: An Essay
author: Gilad Bracha
description: Published March 2025 — An essay by Gilad Bracha reflecting on the 30th anniversary of Java, its evolution, language design trade-offs between C++ and Smalltalk, cultural artifacts in programming, and generics.

title: We Must Pace the Frontier
author: Dario Amodei
description: An essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on why frontier AI scaling demands deliberate pacing, third-party evaluations, and responsible capability management.

title: Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026
author: Anthropic
description: Case studies from threat actors disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026 across seven areas of harm, from cyber operations and multi-agent kill chains to biological misuse.

title: I can’t keep track of the AI stack anymore
author: Sharon Goldman
description: Nvidia is buying Hugging Face. OpenAI is building chips. Databricks, Salesforce and ServiceNow are sprawling across the AI technology stack. Good luck putting any of them in a box.

title: Architecture and model diffs via code conventions
author: Nick Tune
description: Generating architecture diffs for your PRs based on strong codebase conventions

title: No, local models will not win (opinion)
author: Sean Goedecke
description: Analyzes why frontier cloud models will retain a decisive capability and economic edge over locally-run models despite advances in open-weight releases and consumer hardware.

title: The quality paradox of AI-generated code
author: Brian Houck
description: Analyzing telemetry across 500+ engineering organizations, this piece explains why code maintainability (+3.8%) and change confidence (-6.1%) decoupled in Q2 2026. Using the academic TRUCE framework, it shows how AI improves local plausibility while accelerating cognitive and architectural debt.

title: An Accidental Blackboard
author: Giles Edwards-Alexander
description: Thoughtworks assembled 10 engineers in Barcelona to build a mission-critical airline irregular operations (IROps) system using 'hyper-agentic' workflows. In doing so, they accidentally re-discovered the classic AI Blackboard architectural pattern for coordinating autonomous agents through a shared, observable workspace.

title: The Psychology of Software Teams
author: Cat Hicks
description: To build the future, we need new ways of supporting software teams. Explores the psychology that creates resilience, psychological safety, and sustainable high performance in engineering organizations.

title: AI Codecon: Building with Open Source AI
author: O'Reilly
description: Join leading developers and technical experts at our virtual conference series to learn how AI is shaping new workflows, tools, and ways of building software. August 31, 2026.

title: Agentic Engineering
author: Addy Osmani
description: Code generation has become cheap. Verification has not. As AI agents take on more of the development process, the bottleneck has moved from writing code to deciding what to build, directing agents to build it, and being able to answer for what ships.

title: Quantum for Programmers
We turned off Pub/Sub and nobody noticed
author: incident.io
description: Our entire event-driven platform ran through a single message broker, which made it a single point of failure. So we added a second one. This is the story of building an event load balancer, the queueing theory behind it, and the chaos test where we turned off Pub/Sub in production and nobody noticed.

title: AI engineering for critical systems
author: Dan Anthony
description: AI makes code cheap, but critical systems still have to be landed, not just launched. On shifting bottlenecks, changing roles, risk posture, and the atrophy problem - cognitive debt and skill loss in the systems millions depend on.

title: 100 Most-Watched Software Engineering conference talks of 2026
author: Tech Talks Weekly
description: Happy Friday 👋 and welcome to a very special edition of Tech Talks Weekly! Below, you’ll find the 100 most-watched software engineering conference talks published so far in 2026 ranked by view count.

title: Fine-Tuned Lie Detectors Failed to Generalize
author: Jack Hopkins, Dipika Khullar, Rowan Wang, Fabien Roger
description: We trained lie detectors on on-policy lies from open-source models, but fine-tuning them didn’t generalize well to out-of-distribution cases. In these cases, fine-tuned detectors barely beat prompted baselines, and larger prompted models often beat them outright.

title: Regenerative Software
author: O'Reilly
description: A guide to building software architectures that adapt, heal, and evolve over time.

title: Building Resilient Distributed Systems
author: O'Reilly
description: Patterns and practices for building and operating resilient distributed systems.

title: Enforced application architecture for agents and humans
author: Nick Tune
description: Enforcing application architecture instead of relying on markdown files

title: Five Programming Books That Changed How I Think
author: Adam Tornhill
description: A look beyond the usual top five to discover other books that are profoundly novel. Each book influenced how I think about code.

title: Learning Embabel by building with it
author: Zakaria
description: A structured learning path for building with the Embabel agentic framework, covering planning, testing without a model, tools usage, human-in-the-loop controls, tracing, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration.

title: Should we still design code for humans?
author: Valentina Servile
description: Argues that even when AI writes the code, designing readable and maintainable code for humans remains essential to prevent complete loss of system comprehension and avoid giving full autonomy to agents.

title: Agents on the JVM with Embabel - 1.0 GA
author: Embabel
description: A framework for authoring agentic flows on the JVM that seamlessly mix LLM-prompted interactions with code and domain models, offering intelligent path finding toward goals.

title: Control the ideas, not the code
author: Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez)
description: Argues that in the AI era, reviewing AI-generated code line-by-line is suboptimal and often pointless. Programmers should instead focus on controlling high-level design, conducting QA, and building robust test suites.

title: Five studies changing how I think about AI in software engineering
author: Abi Noda (GetDX)
description: Examines five empirical studies on AI's impact on software engineering, noting that while AI compresses upstream work (coding), it increases the downstream burden of verification, testing, and system complexity.

title: AI For Smarties
author: Bertrand Meyer
description: A clear and serious introduction to artificial intelligence, neural networks, and Large Language Models, focusing on separating enduring scientific ideas from current market hype and explaining what can and cannot be guaranteed.

title: Learning AI-Native Software Engineering
author: Alfonso Graziano
description: A practical guide to AI-Native Engineering, covering context engineering, spec-driven development, Model Context Protocol, and agent orchestration for production software.

title: Frontier engineering
author: Clare Liguori
description: A practitioner’s guide to frontier engineering. Ten principles for working with AI agents and shipping dramatically faster.
